Part 1: IMAGE WARPING and MOSAICING

A.1: Shoot the Pictures

I use nine of my photographs in three overlapping sets. The middle photograph in each set is the reference: all other image coordinates are mapped into its coordinate system. I use visually selected correspondences in Part 1 and automatic feature matches in Part 2.

SceneSource photographsReference
Noticeboard1483, 1485, 14871485
Brick wall1511, 1512, 15131512
Atrium1497, 1499, 15011499

I keep the original photographs in the submission. For processing, I apply EXIF orientation, resize the longest dimension to 1024 pixels, and divide RGB values by 255. Each working image has width 768 and height 1024 pixels. The coordinates in the point file refer to these working images.

I measure horizontally to the right and vertically downwards. The center of the top-left pixel is . Thus a point is stored at array row , column . The three source panels below are shown in file order.

A.1: Camera Motion and Overlap

The homography summary, Section 2.3, gives the following formulas for pure camera rotation. I keep its symbols and matrix order, with explicit multiplication dots.

and are the camera intrinsic matrices; rotates rays from camera 1 to camera 2. These formulas assume zero camera translation. A planar surface also supports a homography between its two views. I estimate from image correspondences; I do not estimate camera calibration or rotation separately.

The board and brick wall are approximately planar. The atrium has several depths. I did not measure the optical center during capture, so the photographs do not establish exact pure rotation. The atrium contains visible depth-dependent misalignment, quantified in B.4.

A.2: Recover Homographies

I implement the required function computeH. It takes two lists of corresponding image points and returns a homography matrix. I follow the zero-based matrix subscripts used in the stitching lecture, slides 22–23. The homography summary uses one-based subscripts for the same entries; the bottom-right entry is the same scale parameter in both notations.

In the lecture equation , the source point is and the target point is . The scalar accounts for homogeneous scale. This means multiplication gives scaled coordinates; I must divide by the third coordinate to obtain pixel coordinates.

These are the coordinate equations on stitching slide 22. Adding multiplication dots does not change them. The three entries in the middle column multiply the source vertical coordinate: the first affects the horizontal numerator, the second affects the vertical numerator, and the third affects the common denominator. They are transformation coefficients, not errors or a separate list of point coordinates.

A homography has eight independent parameters because multiplying all nine entries by the same nonzero scale leaves the pixel coordinates unchanged. Setting the bottom-right entry to one gives the eight-unknown parameterization requested in A.2. This parameterization assumes that entry is nonzero before scaling.

A.2: Deriving the Linear Equations

First, multiply each coordinate equation by its common denominator, exactly as on stitching slide 22:

Next, set , move the terms containing the other eight unknowns to the left, and keep the measured target coordinate on the right:

Each correspondence contributes two rows, not one. Stacking correspondences forms , with of size and of size . Four well-positioned point pairs are the minimum; I use 12–15 pairs for each manual mosaic link.

Stitching slides 23–24 also show the homogeneous nine-unknown system . Fixing the last coefficient to one and moving its column to the right gives the eight-unknown system required by this assignment. Under noise, these differently constrained least-squares objectives need not produce identical estimates. I use the assignment’s eight-unknown method consistently.

For every pair, I show numbered corresponding landmarks, their measured coordinates, the recovered matrix and pixel errors. The complete coefficient matrices are also supplied as CSV files.

Substitution into the two rearranged equations gives:

The corresponding two rows of the system are:

The first row controls the predicted horizontal coordinate. Its middle three zeros occur because that equation contains none of the second-row homography coefficients. The second equation similarly has zeros in its first three positions. The final two columns couple source coordinates with the perspective denominator.

The next page displays the full system for all 12 measured pairs. The last column is the right-hand side, not an additional unknown. Odd-numbered rows use the target horizontal coordinate; even-numbered rows use the target vertical coordinate.

A.2: Least-Squares Solution and Verification

Stitching slide 25 gives the least-squares solution below. In this application the unknown vector is the eight homography coefficients. I show the normal-equation formula to explain the calculation; the code uses NumPy’s least-squares solver directly to avoid explicitly inverting the normal-equation matrix.

The stationary condition is . Here has rank 8, so the eight-parameter least-squares solution is unique. I reshape the eight coefficients into the first eight positions of and place 1 in its bottom-right entry.

This matrix maps coordinates in photo 1483 into photo 1485. To verify the first measured pair, I multiply the source coordinate vector and divide by the third component:

The predicted point is (139.243514, 430.936872), close to the measured target (139, 431). I retain full precision for calculations; displayed matrices are rounded. The matrix condition number is 2.476e+07, and the algebraic residual norm is 3.880942. A large condition number indicates sensitivity to coordinate perturbations. This implementation does not use Hartley normalization.

A.2: Calculating Reprojection Error

Reprojection error measures how far a transformed source point falls from its measured target. A hat denotes a predicted coordinate. I first divide by homogeneous scale, then subtract the measured coordinates. These are forward errors in target-image pixels.

The negative vertical residual means the predicted point is slightly above the measured one, because image row coordinates increase downwards. Squared error has units of pixels squared; its square root has units of pixels.

RMSE is the square root of the mean squared distance; it is not the mean distance. The homography summary’s Section 2.6 defines symmetric transfer error by adding the reverse-direction error. My tables use forward error only, matching the implementation and RANSAC threshold. I do not label it as symmetric error.

A.3: Warp the Images

Warping creates an output image in a new coordinate system. Forward mapping can leave holes after rounding. I therefore visit every output pixel and use the inverse homography to find where to sample its color in the source image, as required by A.3.

Let be the output column and row. If the canvas begins at reference coordinate , its reference-coordinate location is . The inverse calculation is:

I sample the source at the resulting continuous coordinate. If the point lies outside the source or the denominator is effectively zero, I mark the output pixel invalid. A separate validity mask ensures that a genuine black pixel is still included.

For nearest-neighbor interpolation, I select the closest pixel center:

The floor brackets mean round down to an integer. For bilinear interpolation, I use the four surrounding pixel centers. Let , , and . The four weights are:

The weights sum to one. I apply the same weighted sum independently to red, green and blue. At the last row or column, I clamp the second neighbor to the last valid pixel. These equations expand the assignment’s nearest-neighbor and four-neighbor weighted-average instructions.

A.3: Interpolation Quality and Speed

RectificationNearest (ms)Bilinear (ms)Time ratio
01 board29.7555.591.87
02 map29.5450.141.70

I time five repeats after one warm-up and report the median on the current machine. Both methods use the same matrix and output dimensions. Nearest neighbor needs one source sample and produces sharper pixel blocks and jagged diagonal edges. Bilinear combines four samples, takes longer in these measurements, and smooths edges but may blur small text. Neither method restores missing detail; strong minification can still alias without a suitable image pyramid.

A.4: Blend the Images into a Mosaic

A mosaic is one larger picture assembled from overlapping photographs. Blending computes a color in each overlap from several aligned images so that a hard boundary is less visible. I first find a common canvas, then warp the source colors and their weights into it, and finally divide their weighted color sum by the total weight.

I transform the four corners , , and of each source image into reference coordinates. Here and denote image width and height; without this subscript denotes a homography. I divide by homogeneous scale before measuring the bounds.

The minimum and maximum range over all transformed corners. Ceiling brackets mean round up. Negative coordinates are allowed in the reference frame: they simply lie left of or above the reference image. I use the union of manual and automatic bounds to make their comparisons use the same canvas.

SceneMinimum Width × height
bulletin board(-302, -373)1602 × 1704
brick wall(-85, -68)949 × 1157
atrium(-171, -111)1087 × 1252

For the noticeboard, the combined bounds are from −302 to 1299 horizontally and from −373 to 1330 vertically. The extra one includes both endpoint pixel centers:

If the homogeneous denominator changes sign across an image, its projection crosses infinity and finite corner bounds are not valid. I reject that case. I also reject a nonpositive canvas or one exceeding 40 million pixels before allocating it.

For the board, this translation adds 302 to every horizontal reference coordinate and 373 to every vertical reference coordinate. It shifts the reference photo as well as the other photos:

The rightmost matrix acts first: the source is mapped into reference coordinates, then translated into the canvas. For inverse sampling, this becomes:

A.4: Computing Blending Weights and Colors

Stitching slide 150 encodes a weighted color as an alpha-premultiplied RGB vector. I use the same accumulate-then-normalize procedure:

To construct the weights, I use a linear distance-to-nearest-edge rule. The following definition is an implementation choice for the feathering described in A.4, rather than a separately stated lecture identity:

For a 100 × 100 image, a pixel at (0, 49) has distance 1 and a pixel at (49, 49) has distance 50. The maximum is 50, so their weights are 0.02 and 1.00. The one-pixel floor avoids discarding the outer boundary when only one image covers it.

I inverse-warp each weight map with the same homography used for its image. Let denote its warped weight, a validity mask (1 for a valid source sample, 0 otherwise), and its warped RGB value. Then the implemented version of the lecture average is:

If only one image contributes, its weight cancels and its color is retained. If the denominator is zero, no source covers the pixel: the RGB preview is black, and the RGBA output is transparent there. A black source pixel remains valid. I blend stored RGB values without exposure compensation or linear-light conversion.

I demonstrate the weighted-color calculation at reference coordinate (389, 524) using board photos 1483 and 1485. This two-image example explains the arithmetic; the final mosaic includes all three valid sources at each location.

Hard overwrite takes the latest image’s color wherever it exists and can create an abrupt brightness boundary. Feather blending transitions gradually across the overlap. It reduces seams but cannot correct duplicate edges caused by a wrong geometric alignment.

A.4: Bulletin Board Mosaic

The poster corners and central wall align well. Small discrepancies remain at the ceiling and floor, which may lie away from the fitted wall plane. Feathering reduces brightness boundaries.

A.4: Brick Wall Mosaic

The main brick joints are broadly continuous. Some near-rail edges remain doubled. Repeated bricks can produce ambiguous correspondences, and the high overlap adds only a modest new field of view.

The canvas is 949 × 1157 pixels. Invalid outer regions are retained to show the complete footprint. A transparent RGBA version is supplied as well.

A.4: Atrium Mosaic

The middle-distance and far structures align more consistently than the near beam and stairs. Thin duplicate edges remain across depths. This is a limitation of fitting one global homography per source; blending cannot remove it.

The canvas is 1087 × 1252 pixels. Invalid outer regions are retained to show the complete footprint. A transparent RGBA version is supplied as well.

PART 2: FEATURE MATCHING for AUTOSTITCHING

B.1: Harris Corner Detection

I use the teacher-provided harris.py without changing any bytes. It operates at one scale, discards a 20-pixel border, and returns corner coordinates in row–column order. My wrapper converts them to horizontal–vertical order for the rest of the pipeline.

The feature lecture, slide 39, gives the determinant-over-trace corner response:

In that slide, is a local second-moment matrix, not the image homography used in Part 1. The two eigenvalues describe intensity variation in two directions. A corner has substantial variation in both directions.

The supplied code calls the epsilon-stabilized detector. Its actual response is shown separately below, using for the local second-moment matrix to avoid confusing it with a homography:

The Gaussian window has standard deviation one. The factor two and small denominator stabilizer are part of the supplied implementation. They are not silently substituted into the lecture identity. I use this supplied response consistently for corner selection.

I then implement adaptive non-maximal suppression (ANMS). It keeps spatially separated strong corners rather than allowing the most textured area to dominate. For each point, I find the nearest point whose response is sufficiently stronger:

If no sufficiently stronger point exists, . I retain the 500 largest radii, or all candidates if fewer than 500 exist. Response and original index break ties. This direct loop is quadratic in candidate count but straightforward to inspect.

B.2: Feature Descriptor Extraction

I extract an axis-aligned 8 × 8 descriptor from a larger 40 × 40 neighborhood, as required. I first blur the grayscale image, then sample every fifth pixel from the local neighborhood. The blur reduces aliasing before subsampling.

The separable Gaussian filter uses and integer offsets from −6 to 6. I normalize the coefficients so that they sum to one:

I implement horizontal and vertical convolution passes with reflection padding. For a feature at (x, y), the 40 × 40 window spans source coordinates x − 20 through x + 19 and y − 20 through y + 19. Within this window I sample row and column indices 2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27, 32 and 37.

Let the 64 samples be . Bias/gain normalization subtracts their mean and divides by their population standard deviation:

I flatten the normalized 8 × 8 array in row order. I reject a patch if its standard deviation is below one millionth, which avoids magnifying numerical noise in a nearly constant patch. I omit rotation alignment and wavelets, as permitted by the assignment.

For positive gain and bias , transformed samples satisfy , and . Substitution explains the invariance:

This normalization does not remove arbitrary changes of rotation, scale, viewpoint or clipping. These equations expand the required bias/gain normalization and Gaussian sampling steps.

B.2: Complete Descriptor Normalization Example

B.2: Examples of Extracted Features

All normalized descriptor displays use the same range from −3 to 3. Clipping applies only to visualization; matching uses the full stored values. These feature patches describe local image appearance rather than physical object identities.

B.3: Feature Matching

I compare each source descriptor with every descriptor in the reference image. Feature lecture slide 105 defines the ratio between the first and second nearest-neighbor distances:

is the source descriptor, the closest target descriptor and the second-closest target descriptor. The prime on the latter distinguishes a candidate; it is not a derivative. A small ratio means the best match is substantially closer than the alternative.

My code saves squared Euclidean distances, also called sum of squared differences (SSD). I show the relationship explicitly so the lecture ratio and implementation threshold are not confused:

I use Brown et al.’s Figure 6b, named in the assignment, for the distinctiveness-ratio idea; 0.65 on squared distances is my fixed implementation choice. The following threshold test uses the same board image pair, RANSAC seed and settings. I do not describe 0.65 as a universal cutoff.

SSD ratio limitMatchesInliersInlier RMSE (px)
0.474601.101
0.55106801.220
0.65126891.237
0.8162971.255

I reject a second-best SSD at or below one trillionth because identical candidates are ambiguous. If several source features choose the same target, I keep the pair with the lowest ratio. I apply the same settings to all six image pairs.

B.3: A Feature-Distance Calculation

For source descriptor 54 in photo 1483, the best target is descriptor 42 in photo 1485. Descriptor indices start at zero. For each of 64 positions, I subtract the target descriptor entry from the source entry, square the difference, and add the terms.

Both forms accept the same match. A second candidate that is almost as close would produce a ratio near one and be rejected. Every one of the 64 squared-difference terms is saved for the best and second-best matches, so the SSD sums can be checked without inferring them from a plot.

B.4: RANSAC for Robust Homography

I implement four-point RANSAC from scratch. It repeatedly estimates a candidate homography from four distinct correspondences, tests all proposed matches, and retains the candidate supported by the largest consistent subset. This follows the sampling, scoring and refitting procedure in the transformation lecture.

StepImplementation
1. SampleDraw four distinct match indices without replacement. Use seed 42.
2. CheckReject a sample if any three source points or any three target points are nearly collinear, or if the system is rank-deficient.
3. FitEstimate the eight-unknown homography with computeH.
4. ScoreMap every source match into the target image. A point is an inlier if its forward error is strictly below 3 pixels.
5. SelectKeep the largest inlier count; use lower median inlier error to break a tie. Repeat for 2000 attempted samples.
6. RefitFit least squares to the consensus, recompute membership, and repeat until stable or five refits. Retain the last valid model.

The collinearity check compares twice the triangle area with one pixel squared. The absolute determinant below is twice the area, with point coordinates measured in pixels:

I save the exact points used in the final least-squares fit separately from the final threshold membership. These may differ if the five-refit limit is reached. A valid consensus establishes consistency with one model, not a guarantee of correct alignment at every depth.

B.4: Choosing the Number of RANSAC Trials

Transformation slide 164 uses success probability , outlier fraction , minimal sample size and trial count . I keep those symbols in its formula:

The reasoning is: one sample is entirely inliers with probability approximately the inlier fraction raised to the sample size. The chance that all trials fail is the single-trial failure probability raised to the number of trials:

For a four-point homography, a 50% outlier fraction and 99% desired success probability, I calculate and round up:

The smallest observed consensus fraction is 88/142 for photo 1497 to photo 1499. Treating that observed subset as inliers gives the illustrative outlier estimate below; it is not ground truth.

Because the implementation samples four distinct indices, the exact probability under a fixed, known consensus is a ratio of combinations. A combination counts unordered subsets:

I use 2000 attempted samples for every pair. Invalid samples count toward this limit. These probabilities are planning models: a consensus can include incorrect matches, an all-inlier sample can be geometrically degenerate, and a single homography can fail on a scene with parallax.

B.4: Bulletin Board — Manual and Automatic Mosaics

The poster corners and central wall align well. Small discrepancies remain at the ceiling and floor, which may lie away from the fitted wall plane. Feathering reduces brightness boundaries.

Both results use reference 1485 and a 1602 × 1704 canvas. Automatic stitching reuses Part 1 warping and blending; only the correspondence estimation changes.

B.4: Brick Wall — Manual and Automatic Mosaics

The main brick joints are broadly continuous. Some near-rail edges remain doubled. Repeated bricks can produce ambiguous correspondences, and the high overlap adds only a modest new field of view.

Both results use reference 1512 and a 949 × 1157 canvas. Automatic stitching reuses Part 1 warping and blending; only the correspondence estimation changes.

B.4: Atrium — Manual and Automatic Mosaics

The middle-distance and far structures align more consistently than the near beam and stairs. Thin duplicate edges remain across depths. This is a limitation of fitting one global homography per source; blending cannot remove it.

Both results use reference 1499 and a 1087 × 1252 canvas. Automatic stitching reuses Part 1 warping and blending; only the correspondence estimation changes.

B.4: What Outlier Rejection Changes

As a baseline, I fit one homography to every ratio-accepted match without RANSAC. I then measure forward errors on the same tentative matches. The table compares the baseline median error and the number of correspondences within the common 3-pixel threshold.

Source / referenceAll-match fit: median (px)All-match fit: inliersRANSAC: inliers
1483 / 1485193.18089
1487 / 1485100.23069
1511 / 15126.6125245
1513 / 15123.07150279
1497 / 149972.58088
1501 / 1499246.20073

The all-match fit is pulled by outliers and generally produces poor alignment. RANSAC finds a more consistent subset before least-squares refitting. I do not compare an all-match median with an inlier-only RMSE as though they were the same accuracy statistic.

The ratio test evaluates descriptor distinctiveness. RANSAC evaluates geometric agreement. Both are needed: repeated texture can survive the appearance test, and a repeated geometric pattern may still support an incorrect model.

B.4: Remaining Alignment Errors and What I Learned

I separately measured two bolt centers on the near beam in photos 1501 and 1499; they were not used in the manual fit. Their forward errors under the automatic homography are 43.97 and 45.36 pixels. Thus low automatic inlier RMSE does not establish good alignment at the near beam.

The manual points mainly cover middle-distance and far structures; automatic RANSAC also selects a locally consistent subset. Different depths can disagree when the camera translates. Point measurement uncertainty and lens distortion can contribute as well. The board and wall are better suited to a global planar model than the atrium.

The most important thing I learned is that a small fitting error is a statement about a particular point set, not the entire image. Clear correspondence selection, inverse sampling and blending have distinct roles: geometry aligns structures, interpolation assigns sampled colors, and blending softens color transitions. Improved fixed-center capture is the most direct way to reduce the observed parallax.
